analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal backstop so insurers must cover pandemic business-closure losses, with taxpayers paying most large claims.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a vote: referred to the House Financial Services Committee on May 22, 2020, it never received a hearing, markup, or floor action before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set up a federal reinsurance program in the Treasury Department for pandemics. Insurers that join must offer pandemic business-interruption coverage in every business interruption policy they sell, and the government would pay 95% of covered losses above each insurer's deductible once industry-wide losses from one emergency pass $250 million, with total federal liability capped at $750 billion a year. It would also strike virus exclusions from business interruption policies already in force, so businesses that bought the coverage before insurers broadly excluded virus losses would be paid in a future pandemic. The program would run through 2027, and the Government Accountability Office would study whether such coverage is available and affordable.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that hold or buy business interruption insurance — restaurants, retailers, hotels, event venues, manufacturers — would gain a way to be paid for losses from government-ordered pandemic shutdowns, which in 2020 most policies excluded. Participating insurers gain a federal backstop that covers 95% of their pandemic losses above a deductible set at 5% of their prior-year premiums, limiting their own downside.

how_it_helps.text: The federal government would pay 95% of an insurer's covered pandemic losses above its deductible — 5% of the prior year's premiums — once industry-wide losses from a covered emergency exceed $250 million [S3].

Participating insurers must offer, in every business interruption policy, pandemic coverage on terms that do not differ materially from coverage for other perils, so the coverage would become standard rather than a special add-on [S3].

The bill voids any exclusion in existing business interruption policies that excludes losses covered by the program, unless the policyholder affirmatively agrees to reinstate it — undoing the virus exclusions insurers added across the market [S3].

The bill requires insurers to clearly disclose to policyholders the premium for the federally backed coverage and the existence of the $750 billion annual cap, and lets insurers no longer be liable above their deductible once losses pass that cap [S3].

The Government Accountability Office must study where business interruption insurance is hard to get or unaffordable, and the Treasury Department must report annually on the program's pricing, take-up rates, and effectiveness [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the tail risk: in a severe pandemic the Treasury pays 95% of business interruption claims above insurers' deductibles, up to $750 billion a year, with no dedicated funding source specified in the bill. Insurers lose on their existing book, since virus exclusions in policies already sold would be voided. Businesses would also pay premiums for the mandated coverage offer.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, and insurers on old policies

drawbacks.text: The program puts a large contingent cost on the federal government: it would cover 95% of pandemic business losses once a low $250 million trigger is passed, capped only at $750 billion per year, effectively making taxpayers the reinsurer of last resort for a risk the private market had priced as uninsurable [S3].

Voiding virus exclusions in existing policies retroactively rewrites contracts that insurers sold on the assumption virus losses were not covered, a cost the industry argued would land on the companies and their other policyholders [S3].

Because the federal share only pays insurers after they pay claims, and insurers would face the mandate to cover losses they had excluded, premiums for business interruption coverage would likely rise, a cost passed through to the businesses the bill is meant to help [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real protection to businesses against a catastrophic, previously uninsured risk, and it follows the model of the existing federal terrorism risk backstop. But the design leans heavily toward the industry: taxpayers take 95% of the losses past a modest trigger, insurers get a federal floor under a market they had pulled out of, and the retroactive voiding of exclusions is a genuine contractual rewrite that insurers opposed. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the federal share is generous and the funding is open-ended.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2020 and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn Maloney introduced the Pandemic Risk Insurance Act of 2020 on May 22, 2020, with 20 Democratic cosponsors, during the first months of the COVID-19 shutdowns [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the day it was introduced, and the action record shows no hearing, markup, vote, or further action of any kind afterward [S5].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without the bill ever reaching the House floor, so the program was never created [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Property-casualty insurers kept the virus exclusions in their existing policies and avoided a government mandate to offer pandemic coverage on existing terms; taxpayers avoided a contingent federal liability of up to $750 billion a year. Businesses that wanted pandemic coverage got nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and taxpayers; businesses got nothing

for.name: Restaurant, hotel, retail and event-industry businesses
for.role: Business coalition that formed the Business Interruption Group to push for a federal pandemic insurance backstop
for.what_they_did: Lobbied Congress during the 2020 shutdowns to create a federal program so their pandemic closure losses would be insurable

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote; it died in committee

against.name: Property-casualty insurance industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill's retroactive voiding of virus exclusions in existing policies, arguing insurers had sold those policies with pandemic losses excluded, while supporting a forward-looking federal backstop instead

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 20 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and no vote was ever taken on the bill.

industries.note: The bill locks insurers in as the permanent channel for pandemic business interruption coverage, with a federal backstop paying 95% of their losses above a 5%-of-premiums deductible and a government-created market via the coverage mandate. The offsetting cost is that virus exclusions in policies already in force would be voided, and the government would cap their liability at $750 billion a year while taxpayers absorb the rest of the tail risk.

industries.industry: Hospitality, restaurant, retail and event businesses
industries.note: These businesses bore the largest pandemic shutdown losses in 2020 and mostly found their business interruption policies excluded virus losses. The bill would void those exclusions in existing policies and require insurers to offer the coverage going forward, letting them be paid for future government-ordered closures.

The bill explicitly preserves insurers' ability to buy private reinsurance for their deductibles and retained losses, and the mandatory pandemic coverage would expand the pool of risk that reinsurers can wrap.
